recommended: Replace 'any failure = 0, cap D' with three severity tiers taken from how regulators triage hazards. CRITICAL: safety score 0 and the grade is forced to E. Examples: a pathogen detected, melamine, Sudan or other non-permitted toxic dyes, argemone oil, a banned drug or stimulant, or a heavy metal or mycotoxin at 5x its limit or more. SERIOUS: safety score at most 40 and the grade capped at D. Examples: a heavy metal, mycotoxin, pesticide, veterinary drug or preservative over its limit, a faecal or hygiene indicator such as Enterobacteriaceae, coliforms, E. coli or S. aureus over its limit, or adulteration such as foreign fat, sugar syrup or amino-acid spiking. MINOR: FSSAI quality or 'sub-standard' parameters such as moisture, ash, acid value, peroxide value, BR reading, TSS, total plate count or yeast & mould. These cost 15 points each, or 25 if well outside the limit, with no cap. A result moves up a tier only by the over-limit rules given per tier. A result moves down one tier when the lab's own measurement uncertainty puts it within the limit. A verdict printed on the lab report ('unsafe' / 'sub-standard') overrides the keyword tier when it is stricter.
why: Every regulator we checked grades failures by how likely and how serious harm is, not by pass/fail. FDA (21 CFR 7.3(m), 7.41) uses Class I/II/III. EU RASFF records a risk decision of serious / not serious / undecided, with a list of what counts as serious. EU Reg 2073/2005 and FSSAI's microbiological standards split 'food safety criteria' (batch must be withdrawn) from 'process hygiene criteria' (fix the process). The FSS Act separates 'unsafe' (s.3(1)(zz)) from 'sub-standard' (s.3(1)(zx)). It punishes them very differently: s.51 sub-standard is a fine of up to Rs 5 lakh; s.59 unsafe can bring imprisonment that scales with injury, up to life. A blanket 'any failure = 0' treats a slightly high moisture reading like Salmonella. That misleads shoppers in both directions: it overstates quality slips and understates true hazards, since both land at D.

tiers.meaning: Reasonable probability of serious harm or death from eating this product. Matches FDA/FSIS Class I and an EU RASFF 'serious' (alert) risk. Covers pathogens in ready-to-eat food, prohibited or non-permitted toxic substances, and gross exceedances of no-threshold contaminants.
tiers.grade_effect: safety score = 0 and the final grade is forced to E, whatever honesty and nutrition score. Show 'Serious health hazard found' with the parameter.
tiers.over_limit_rule: Pathogens and prohibited substances are critical on any 'detected' / 'present in 25 g' / status=fail, regardless of value/limit; their legal limit is absence or a reference point for action. Escalation INTO critical from serious: a heavy_metal or toxin (mycotoxin) result with value/limit >= 5. Lead, inorganic arsenic and cadmium are IARC 1/2A and aflatoxins IARC 1; JECFA/WHO give no safe threshold for lead or aflatoxin, so exposure and risk rise in proportion. The 5x multiple is OpenLabel policy, not a regulator number (RASFF treats ANY exceedance of a legal limit for these carcinogens as an alert). 'mineral acid' (vinegar, sweets) is placed here because FSSAI forbids it outright; downgrade to serious if a reviewer judges otherwise.
tiers.source: 21 CFR 7.3(m)(1) Class I; FSIS 8080.1 Class I examples (pathogens in RTE, E. coli O157:H7). RASFF SOP 2 alert criteria (a) prohibited substances / RPA reached (chloramphenicol, nitrofurans), (d) IARC 1/2A/2B carcinogens over a legal limit, (f) microbes over EU food safety criteria. EU 2073/2005 food safety criteria (Salmonella, L. monocytogenes, STEC, Cronobacter), whose failure means withdraw/recall. FSS Act s.3(1)(zz)(i) poisonous/deleterious, (v) non-permitted substance, (viii) non-specified colouring matter. WHO 2008 melamine outbreak (infant deaths). WHO lead and mycotoxin fact sheets (no known safe lead level; acute aflatoxicosis can be fatal).

tiers.meaning: Over a legal safety limit, but harm is long-term, dose-dependent, or not probable from normal use. Matches FDA Class II / RASFF 'possibly requires rapid action', and is 'unsafe' under FSS Act s.3(1)(zz)(xii). Also covers hygiene indicators of faecal or post-process contamination, and deliberate adulteration that FSSAI treats as an adulterant.
tiers.grade_effect: safety score = max 40 for the first serious result, minus 10 for each additional one (floor 0). The final grade is capped at D (A/B/C becomes D). Show 'Over the safety limit' with value, limit and multiple.
tiers.over_limit_rule: Base tier on any fail. heavy_metal / toxin with value/limit >= 5 escalates to critical (see critical). Pesticides and veterinary-drug MRL exceedances do NOT escalate on the multiple alone. MRLs are good-agricultural-practice trading limits, not safety limits, and the EU only treats a residue as serious when predicted intake exceeds the ARfD; we cannot compute that without consumption data. Hygiene indicators (Enterobacteriaceae, coliforms, E. coli, S. aureus, B. cereus) do not escalate to critical. They indicate a risk; they do not prove a pathogen. Within the tier, value/limit >= 2 costs an extra 10 points (score 30 instead of 40).
tiers.source: 21 CFR 7.3(m)(2) Class II and 7.41 (likelihood, seriousness, long-range consequences). RASFF SOP 2 'possibly requires rapid action' (a) ML exceedances, (b) unauthorised substances, (d) microbes at levels that significantly increase disease risk; pesticides serious only if short-term intake > ARfD (alert criterion c). FSS Act s.3(1)(zz)(xii) (pesticides/contaminants over regulatory limits = unsafe) and (zz)(iii)/(x) unhygienic or insanitary processing. FSS Act s.3(1)(a) adulterant and s.57 penalty for possessing an adulterant (up to Rs 2 lakh not injurious, Rs 10 lakh injurious). UK HSE and EFSA on MRL exceedance not implying a health concern. EU 2073/2005 and FSSAI process hygiene criteria (E. coli / Enterobacteriaceae / coagulase-positive staphylococci).

tiers.meaning: Quality or composition shortfall: food that is 'sub-standard' under FSS Act s.3(1)(zx) ('does not meet the specified standards but not so as to render the article of food unsafe'). Also general spoilage/process indicators with no direct pathogen link. Matches FDA/FSIS Class III.
tiers.grade_effect: 15 points off the safety score per failed parameter, or 25 if well outside the limit (see rule). Floor 50 from minor results alone. No grade cap. Show 'Below FSSAI quality standard' rather than a safety warning.
tiers.over_limit_rule: For maximum-type limits, value/limit >= 1.5 costs 25 instead of 15. For minimum-type limits (protein, fat, TSS, fruit %, iodine), the trigger is value <= 0.67 x limit. Escalation to serious: value/limit >= 10 for total plate count / yeast & mould (one log over suggests gross insanitary handling or spoilage, FSS Act s.3(1)(zz)(ii)/(x)). Also >= 3x for acid value / peroxide value (decomposition) or acid-insoluble ash (sand/dirt as extraneous matter). These multiples are OpenLabel policy.
tiers.source: FSS Act s.3(1)(zx) sub-standard. Penalty s.51 is a fine only (up to Rs 5 lakh), while s.59 unsafe brings imprisonment, showing the statute's own severity split. 21 CFR 7.3(m)(3) Class III; FSIS 8080.1 Class III example (excess water, economic advantage, no health effect). EU 2073/2005 Art. 7(4) and FSSAI Table 4A: process hygiene failures (aerobic count, yeast & mould) require corrective action, not recall.

fssai_mapping: Steps for classifying a failed result. (1) If the lab report itself states an FSSAI verdict, use it as a floor. 'Unsafe' (FSS Act s.3(1)(zz)) means at least serious. 'Sub-standard' (s.3(1)(zx)) means minor. 'Misbranded' (s.3(1)(zf)) belongs in the honesty part, not safety. (2) Otherwise, match the lowercased parameter text against critical keywords first, then serious, then minor. Match whole words or phrases (regex \b...\b, not substring or prefix) so that: 'urea' does not hit 'urease'; 'lead' does not hit 'misleading'; 'ash' does not hit 'wash'; 'don' does not hit 'condensed'; 'tin' does not hit 'testing'; 'pb' only matches as a token or in '(pb)'; 'coli' alone is never a keyword ('broccoli', 'coliform'); 'sem'/'ahd'/'aoz'/'amoz' (nitrofuran metabolites) only match as whole tokens. Order matters: 'E. coli O157' hits 'o157' (critical) before 'e. coli' (serious); 'Listeria monocytogenes' is critical; 'Sudan I' hits 'sudan' before 'colour'; 'Aflatoxin B1' hits 'aflatoxin' (serious, critical at >= 5x); 'Lead chromate' hits 'chromate' (critical) before 'lead' (serious); 'Free amino acids' in protein powder hits 'free amino' (serious adulteration). (3) If no keyword matches, fall back on the group: heavy_metal, toxin, pesticide and spiking go to serious; other goes to minor. (4) Apply the per-tier over_limit_rule using value/limit. Pathogens and prohibited substances often have no numeric value ('Detected', 'Present/25 g'); status=fail alone makes them critical. (5) Measurement-uncertainty step-down: if the lab reports an expanded uncertainty U and value - U <= limit, drop one tier (critical to serious, serious to minor). Do not apply this to presence/absence pathogens or prohibited substances. Basis: EU Reg 401/2006 rejects a lot only if it exceeds the ML 'beyond reasonable doubt' after measurement uncertainty. In FSSAI terms, everything in critical and serious is 'unsafe' under s.3(1)(zz). The Act does not itself grade unsafe food; it scales punishment by the actual outcome (s.59 no injury / non-grievous / grievous / death). Our critical/serious split mirrors FDA Class I vs II. Note: the FSSAI Food Recall Procedure Regulations 2017 (Gazette text) define NO Class I/II/III. They only speak of the 'relative urgency or gravity of the recall'. So we must not claim an FSSAI recall class; cite FDA/RASFF for the class concept and the FSS Act for unsafe vs sub-standard. Plurals are listed explicitly (e.g. 'coliforms'); an implementation may instead allow an optional trailing 's' in the word-boundary regex.
notes: 1) Code mismatch: backend/grading.py has SAFETY_GROUPS including 'microbiology', but CONTEXT says microbiology results arrive in group 'other'. It also lists 'yeast', 'mould', 'coliform' and 'mineral oil' in SAFETY_WORDS, so today a yeast & mould failure zeroes safety. Under this scheme it is minor. 2) The 'other' group mixes pathogens, hygiene indicators and quality parameters, so classify 'other' by keyword, never by group. 3) Economic adulteration (sugar syrup in honey, foreign fat in ghee, vegetable fat in ice cream, amino spiking in whey) is placed in serious because the FSS Act treats an adulterant as an offence (s.57) and shoppers are buying a fake product. But FSIS lists GRAS economic adulteration (excess water) as Class III, so this is a policy choice. The alternative is to score it in honesty (40%) and leave safety alone; flag it to the user. Hazardous spiking (melamine, Sudan/metanil, argemone, urea/detergent in milk) is critical or serious regardless. 4) The 5x (heavy metal/mycotoxin to critical), 10x (TPC/yeast & mould to serious), 3x (rancidity/ash to serious) and 1.5x/2x point steps are OpenLabel policy. No regulator publishes recall classes by multiple; RASFF alerts on ANY exceedance for IARC 1/2A/2B carcinogens, so a stricter alternative is to make every lead/arsenic/cadmium/aflatoxin exceedance critical. 5) Pesticides: no escalation by multiple because the EU test (intake > ARfD) needs consumption data we lack. A 10x screen could be added later but would be unsourced. 6) Undeclared allergens are Class I/II at FDA/FSIS and a RASFF alert, but none of our result groups carry them; if added, put major allergens (peanut, tree nut, milk, egg, fish, shellfish, sesame) in critical. 7) Infant foods: FDA lead action levels (10/20 ppb) and Codex melamine 1 mg/kg in powdered infant formula are far tighter than general limits. Use the category's own limit from the lab, and treat any serious result in infant_formula / baby food categories as critical (FSIS/FDA 7.41(a)(3) weighs at-risk populations). 8) Not verified: Jan Vishwas 2023 changes to s.59 (secondary only); current EU ACN SOP 2 (I read the 2017 RASFF SOPs under Reg 16/2011); verbatim Codex CXS 193 ALARA preamble and current melamine/aflatoxin ML numbers; FSSAI microbiology Table 4A/4B text (secondary summary only); whether FSIS Directive 8080.1 Rev. 8 keeps the same examples (state copy Rev 8.1 does).
